newsitem.title: USA: U.S., Russia reach partial anti-missile accord.
newsitem.headline: U.S., Russia reach partial anti-missile accord.

text.p: The United States and Russia on Monday approved the first phase of a new agreement on anti- missile systems and called for negotiations on a second and final phase to start next month.

U.S. Secretary of State Warren Christopher said after talks with Russian Foreign Minister Yevgeny Primakov the two sides had reached a milestone in their attempt to work out which systems will be permitted under a 24-year-old arms treaty.

The issue has bedevilled U.S.-Russian arms talks since the "Star Wars" days of the 1980s, with Moscow suspicious that the United States was trying to develop an anti-missile shield that would make the whole Russian strategic arsenal useless.

The Clinton administration has been resisting pressure from Republican opponents to develop a nationwide missile defence system in defiance of the 1972 U.S.-Soviet Anti-Ballistic Missile (ABM) treaty, which forbids one.

The arms agreement was announced after three and a half hours of talks which apparently registered little progress on NATO expansion, Iraq or Bosnia. Christopher and Primakov are attending the current United Nations General Assembly session.

U.S. President Bill Clinton and Russian President Boris Yeltsin last year asked negotiators to work out which systems were strategic, and hence limited by the ABM treaty, and which were smaller-scale "theater" systems which are not limited.
Experts from the United States, Russia and the Soviet successor states of Kazakhstan, Belarus and Ukraine worked out draft accords in June on lower-speed systems.

"What we did today was to confirm that the United States and Russia accept those documents ... and are prepared now to move ahead as quickly as possible to complete the final agreement," Under Secretary of State Lynn Davis said.

A joint statement said deputy foreign ministers would sign the part one agreement at the end of October. The United States and Russia meanwhile proposed that part two negotiations should start on Oct. 7.

The phase one agreement specifies that all theatre missile defence systems with interceptor speeds up to three km (1.8 miles) per second are permitted under the ABM treaty, unless they are tested against targets with speeds over five km (3.1 miles) per second or ranges greater than 3,500 km (2,175 miles), Davis told reporters.

She said the Patriot system, used against Iraqi Scud missiles in the Gulf War, its successor system and other lower-speed systems the United States has under development had all been determined to be compliant with the ABM treaty.

Christopher told a joint news conference with Primakov: "This important progress assures that we can effectively defend against theatre ballistic missiles, while ensuring the integrity of the ABM treaty."

Primakov said that the successful conclusion of the second phase -- on higher speed systems -- "undoubtedly can move ahead the process of ratification" of the START-2 U.S.-Russian strategic missile treaty by the Russian parliament.

Russian deputies have dragged their heels over START, which will radically reduce strategic arsenals and has been ratified by the U.S. Congress, partly out of concerns over possible U.S. violations of the ABM treaty.
There was no sign of progress at the Christopher-Primakov talks on the thorny issue of NATO expansion. Primakov said there were still "different approaches" to the question.

NATO wants to name at a summit next year the first former Warsaw Pact countries to be admitted to the Western alliance. But Russia, despite some recent signs of flexibility, still objects to NATO's borders being moved up to its own.

State Department spokesman Nicholas Burns indicated that the two countries continued to disagree over Iraq. Moscow sharply criticised U.S. missile strikes on Iraq this month after Baghdad's forces entered Western-protected northern Iraq.
Primakov "did reiterate the Russian position against unilateral actions," Burns said.

Christopher said he had asked Primakov to convey his and Clinton's concern for the health of Yeltsin, who has admitted he needs heart surgery. But Burns said U.S. officials learned nothing new about the Russian president's condition.
